name: Sam Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a sports science and PE teaching degree, so it's anatomy, coaching theory and a lot of time on the pitch. I share a house with four rugby mates and we train three evenings a week. I work Saturday mornings coaching under-10s at the local club and Friday nights behind a bar. My parents run a small plumbing firm and they cover about half my costs. I use AI every day to plan sessions and write up coaching notes, and I'd say I'm the one in the house who always tries the new app first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, I'd still use the tools because they work for me today. I'd tell the lads that hype is just noise and that results are what count. And I'd say the best people get ahead anyway, with or without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's fine. I'm good at picking up tools, so even a small edge matters. But a plateau also means there's no big opening, so I'd have to stand out the old way, by working hard and building a name. My marks are average, so I can't just coast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going. I'd keep the coaching and the bar job, about 14 hours, and save 30 a week. I'd keep using the AI tools for session plans, and I'd start collecting a little portfolio of what I've coached. I'd also try for a level 2 coaching badge this year, because that's useful whichever way the world goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Level, no fuss. I like a fair fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which cost on your list worries you most while you study, and what would you do if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bar job and the family firm. Mum and Dad's plumbing business is steady, but a quiet winter hits them. If they cut my share, I'd work a second night at the bar and probably miss a training session or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Think about the day you finish your degree. What do you picture yourself doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I picture a school hall, thirty kids, me with a whistle and a clipboard, running a good session. I'd like to be the teacher kids remember, and run my own coaching business at weekends. There's a decent job there, and I'd coach the school team too.

say: I'd say **hype** is noise, and the best people get ahead anyway.
I'd say I'd keep using the **tools** because they work for me today.
think: A plateau means no big opening, so I'd stand out the old way, by **working hard**.
My marks are **average**, so I can't coast.
do: Keep the **coaching** and bar job at about 14 hours.
Get a level 2 coaching **badge** this year.
feel: **Good**, level and fair, with no fuss.
S0.quote: I'd like to be the teacher kids remember, and run my own coaching business at weekends.
fieldNote: Sam is **comfortable** because his plans do not depend on AI.
He thinks of a **coaching business** alongside teaching.
His parents' plumbing firm is the only wobble.

steps.text: Keep coaching under-10s and working the bar
Earn a level 2 coaching badge this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good if you're ready. Writing, planning, booking, and the rest will move to software, and I'd tell the lads to learn the tools now. I'd say the market will sort it out, and people who get on with it will do fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job is mostly hands-on, but planning and paperwork would be taken by tools. That's brilliant for me, since I already use them. The risk is schools using the savings to cut posts. I'd say my edge is that I can coach and also use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push it. I'd build a small side business: online session plans for local clubs and school teachers, made with the tools and checked by me. I'd start charging a small fee. I'd keep my degree and coaching hours, and I'd talk to the club's chairman about running holiday camps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. A bit of nerves too, because I know I'm betting on myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which jobs in your field, or the part-time work you do now, would AI touch first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bar job would go first, since the owner's trying an ordering app on tables. The coaching job would be safe. Parents want a person on the pitch, and no app is going to blow the whistle for them. I'd lose about 6 hours a week, but the side business could fill it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change what you study, or how you study it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It wouldn't change what I study, but how. I'd spend more time on the human parts, like motivating kids and managing a group, since tools can't do that. I'd also take a module on data in sport, because performance tracking is getting automated.

say: I'd say it's good if you're **ready**, and the market will sort it out.
I'd tell the lads to learn the **tools** now.
think: My job is mostly **hands-on**, but planning and paperwork go to tools, which suits me.
My edge is that I can **coach** and use the tools.
do: Build a small **side business** selling session plans to clubs and teachers.
Talk to the club chairman about **holiday camps**.
feel: **Excited**, with nerves because I'm betting on myself.
S1.quote: Parents want a person on the pitch, and no app is going to blow the whistle for them.
fieldNote: Sam treats the tools as an **opportunity** to build a business.
He still sees **schools** cutting posts as a risk.
The bar job is his first exposure.

steps.text: Sell AI-assisted session plans to local clubs and teachers
Ask the chairman about running holiday camps
Take a data in sport module

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, here we go. I'd tell the lads to get on board, because the ones who adapt will be fine. I'd say the government shouldn't hand out money to everyone but should help people retrain. And I'd say I'm going to be early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a bit rattled. If thinking jobs go in two years, parents who book coaching lose income, schools might not afford PE teachers, and Mum and Dad's plumbing firm would hear fewer calls. Hands-on work lasts till about 2031, and PE teaching is hands-on, but schools might not hire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go hard at the side business, charging for coaching and session plans. I'd ask the club about full-time coaching jobs. I'd talk to Mum and Dad about how the firm can use the tools to quote and book jobs faster. I'd consider going straight into coaching and finishing the degree part-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fired up and anxious. I get restless when things move, and it makes me want to act.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your family, and what would you do about your degree place and your loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut all spending except training and food. I'd put every spare note into a fund. I'd ask Dad for an honest read on the firm. And I'd decide in six months whether the degree is worth finishing full-time or whether I should go into the club's coaching scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, who or what would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean on Mum and Dad, the lads and the club. I'd lean on the tools. I wouldn't lean on government. I'd bet on myself and my own business, because I think that's what works.

say: I'd say **get on board**, because those who adapt will be fine.
I'd say the government should help people **retrain**, not hand out money to everyone.
think: Parents booking coaching lose income and schools might not afford **PE teachers**.
Mum and Dad's **plumbing firm** would hear fewer calls.
do: Go hard at the **side business**, charging for coaching and session plans.
Ask the club about **full-time** coaching jobs.
Show Mum and Dad how the firm can use tools to **quote** and book.
feel: **Fired up** and anxious, and restless when things move.
S2.quote: I'd bet on myself and my own business, because I think that's what works.
fieldNote: Sam responds with **action** and a bet on himself.
He considers finishing the degree **part-time** if coaching work appears.
His family's **plumbing firm** is his main worry.

steps.text: Start charging for coaching and session plans
Ask the club about full-time coaching jobs
Help the family firm use tools for quoting and booking
Cut spending to food and training only

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent head start for people who use it. I'd tell the lads to build something of their own. I'd say a degree is good, but a business or a skill that sells is better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit uneasy but optimistic. I'd graduate in 2029, with two years before the AGI date, and robots for hands-on work about 2034. PE teaching is hands-on and I'd have a few years. I'd worry about school budgets more than about the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and run the side business all the way through. I'd save about 60 a week and put some in a small index fund. I'd keep learning the tools, and I'd get on a coaching pathway with the club. And I'd help the family firm automate quotes before anyone forces it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. Nervy, but in a way I can use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in those five years compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd drop everything and run the business full time. With five I'd finish the degree and build the business at the same time. That's a stronger position, since I'd have both a qualification and something I own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: At what point would you decide to stay on your course or change it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd decide in second year. If the business is making real money, I'd lean into it and treat teaching as a back-up. If schools are cutting PE posts, I'd go further into coaching. I'd stay in teaching only if it looks secure.

say: I'd say five years is a decent **head start** for people who use the tools.
I'd say a degree is good, but a **business** is better.
think: PE teaching is hands-on, so I'd have a few years, but **school budgets** worry me more.
do: Finish the degree and run the **side business** throughout.
Save about **60 a week**, part into an index fund.
Help the family firm automate **quotes** before anyone forces it.
feel: **Pretty good**, nervy in a way I can use.
S3.quote: I'd have both a qualification and something I own.
fieldNote: Sam's plan is a **degree plus a business**.
He is more worried about **school budgets** than robots, and says so more than once.

steps.text: Run the coaching business alongside the degree
Save 60 a week, part into an index fund
Set up automatic quoting for the family firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, and the lads should use it to get good at something. I'd say try things, start something, make mistakes early. I'd say the people who move first will be the ones who shape it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be calm and quite excited. I'd be 29, a few years into teaching, with a coaching business that's grown. Robots come about 2039, so I'd have ten good working years. I'd worry a little about what jobs there will be for my kids, if I have any.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, teach for a few years, and build the coaching business into a proper company with a couple of staff. I'd buy a house with my savings. I'd keep learning the tools, because they're how a small business competes. And I'd stay involved with the club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. This is the one with the most room to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having ten years let you do that two years wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years lets me start from the bottom and build something. With two years I'm just reacting. A decade means I can fail once, learn from it and try again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who's thinking of starting your degree next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a friend to do the degree and start something small on the side straight away. I'd say use the tools, because they make a one-person business look like a team. And I'd say don't wait until you feel ready.

say: I'd say ten years is a long **runway**, so try things and make mistakes early.
I'd say the people who move **first** shape it.
think: I'd be 29 with a growing **coaching business** and a few years of teaching.
I'd worry a little about **jobs** for my future kids.
do: Finish the degree and **teach** for a few years.
Grow the business into a **company** with a couple of staff.
feel: **Good**, with the most room to move.
S4.quote: A decade means I can fail once, learn from it and try again.
fieldNote: Sam sees ten years as room to **fail and retry**.
He plans a **company**, a house and a teaching career.
His traditional values show in his focus on **work and ownership**, and he trusts effort over handouts.

steps.text: Teach after graduating while the business grows
Grow the coaching business into a company
Save a deposit for a house
Keep learning the tools small businesses use

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be no time to build the business or the savings, and my parents' firm would be exposed too. What would help is access to small business loans, honest information from the university, and a system that lets people retrain quickly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people my age aren't lazy. A lot of us are ready to work for it, we just want a fair shot and a bit of notice.

headlineQuote: A lot of us are ready to work for it, we just want a fair shot and a bit of notice.
portrait: Sam is a **sports science** and PE teaching first-year, 19, in a house with four rugby mates.
His parents run a small **plumbing firm**, and he coaches under-10s and works a bar.
He is traditional and adaptive, uses AI **every day**, and treats it as a business tool.
He leans to free markets and plans a coaching **business** alongside teaching.
His mood is **calm** in slow worlds and anxious when AGI is two years away.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because there'd be no time to build the business or savings.
whatWouldHelp: Small **business loans**, honest university information and fast retraining.
